title: After 200+ iOS games, the biggest benefit of AI development for me is the shorter feedback loop
author: Zestyclose-Use9011
selftext:
I've made more than 200 iOS games, and Apple has featured 18 of them. I don't write code. I used Buildbox, and now I'm using AI to help build a browser game called KlipZi City.



The part that's made me excited again is the loop between an idea and a playable change.



I describe what I want, AI helps implement it, then I play it and decide what needs changing. Being able to publish a tested browser update without another app-store submission changes how that feels. I can keep working on an idea while it's still fresh.



The first playable prototype took 37 minutes. That was the beginning. The game people can play now has had weeks of further development, testing and fixes. Fast generation doesn't mean I can skip deciding whether something works or is fun.



I also wanted to experiment with monetisation. Playing stays free, while optional names, billboards, shopfronts and characters can be bought inside the city. Billboards are still ads. The experiment is whether the revenue model can fit into the world without repeatedly stopping play. I'm not claiming proven commercial success.



My prediction is that more people will make small games for themselves and their communities, even if those games would never make sense to a traditional publisher.



I'm much less certain about when AI could produce something genuinely AAA in minutes. That prediction isn't necessary for this smaller change to matter.



For those building this way, has the shorter feedback loop actually improved your game, or have you mainly ended up with more prototypes to maintain?



Disclosure: I'm KlipZi City's creator. The game is AI-assisted, and I used AI to help edit this post from my own thoughts and experience.
